    Important Words
    • kaṇṭaka-viddha-aṅgaḥ — one whose body has been pinpricked
      Compound: kaṇṭaka (thorn, pin) + viddha (pierced) + aṅga (body). The compact image carries the whole teaching — only the body that has known the pin reads the other's wince correctly. Gauḍīya devotees treasure this as the basis for kāruṇya.
    • vyathām — pain
      Accusative of vyathā. The same word used in SB 1.8.51 by Kuntī when she requests calamities (so she may always remember Kṛṣṇa). The verse here uses vyathā ethically; Kuntī uses it devotionally — both as Bhagavān-pointing instruments.
    • jīva-sāmyam — equality of jīvas
      Compound: jīva + sāmya (sameness). Gauḍīya frame: all jīvas are equal as parts of Kṛṣṇa (mamaivāṁśo jīva-loke); their bodily form differs, their svarūpa does not. Empathy follows from tattva, not sentiment.
    • aviddha-kaṇṭakaḥ — one not pricked by a pin
      Compound: a- (not) + viddha (pierced) + kaṇṭaka (pin). The man whom suffering has spared cannot read it in another. The verse withholds judgment — it simply describes a structural limit. Sat-saṅga is what supplies the missing wound vicariously.
    By seeing their faces, one whose body has been pricked by pins can understand the pain of others who are pinpricked. Realizing that this pain is the same for everyone, he does not want others to suffer in this way. But one who has never been pricked by pins cannot understand this pain.
    Purport

    There is a saying, “The happiness of wealth is enjoyable by a person who has tasted the distress of poverty.” There is also another common saying, vandhyā ki bujhibe prasava-vedanā: “A woman who has not given birth to a child cannot understand the pain of childbirth.” Unless one comes to the platform of actual experience, one cannot realize what is pain and what is happiness in this material world. The laws of nature act accordingly. If one has killed an animal, one must himself be killed by that same animal. This is called māṁsa. Mām means “me,” and sa means “he.” As I am eating an animal, that animal will have the opportunity to eat me. In every state, therefore, it is ordinarily the custom that if a person commits murder he is hanged.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    By seeing their faces, one whose body has been pricked by pins can understand the pain of others who are pinpricked. Realizing that this pain is the same for everyone, he does not want others to suffer in this way. But one who has never been pricked by pins cannot understand this pain.
    Commentary

    By seeing the symptoms (lingaih), such as withering of the face, one develops sympathy with others, understands their pain, having experienced it oneself. One who has not experienced being pierced by a thorn (aviddha kanthaka) cannot understand others pain.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The reason is given. One does not desire that the pain experienced by another being whose limb is pierced by a thorn should continue, since by seeing the symptoms like a contorted face, one attains a similar state of pain. Remembering one’s own pain one manifests mercy. Aviddha-kaṇṭakaḥ means “a person who has not been pierced by a thorn.” The members of the compound are reversed as in rāja-danta (principal tooth). Or it can mean “a person to whom thorns are not attached.”

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    One who is not being pierced by a thorn does not desire the pain of a living being pierced by a thorn. Though one develops sympathy for another person, by seeing symptoms in the person’s limbs, he does not become similar to the person pierced, but desires that. A poor man, seeing his own suffering, sees such suffering in others.

    Personal Guidance
    Real compassion for others is born from your own tasted pain — let what has pricked you teach you never to inflict that prick on another soul.
    Practical Applications
    • Recall one specific suffering you have personally tasted, and today refuse to inflict that exact pain on anyone within your reach.
    • Notice when you dismiss another's complaint as exaggeration — pause, and ask whether you are simply someone 'never pricked by that pin.'
    • Before eating, speaking, or acting today, apply the māṁsa test: would I accept this being done to me? If not, withdraw the act and offer the moment to Kṛṣṇa.
    Analogy

    Two men walk barefoot through a thornbush. The first has been pricked a hundred times and steps gently around the others. The second has soft shoes and tramples through — the cries he hears below his feet are abstractions to him. Empathy is a wound that has learned its lesson.

    Stories
    Yudhiṣṭhira's reluctance to rule

    After the Kurukṣetra war Yudhiṣṭhira refused to take the throne. He had seen the cost — his own kin slaughtered, women widowed, children orphaned — and he could not bear to inflict any future suffering even by the legitimate exercise of kingly daṇḍa.

    Kṛṣṇa, Bhīṣma, and Vyāsa had to instruct him at length (Śānti-parva, Anuśāsana-parva) precisely because his ātma-aupamya had become so sharp it threatened the rāja-dharma needed to protect dharma itself. SB 10.10.14's principle made flesh, and its limit also addressed: empathy must be channeled by śāstra, not run wild.

    Important Words
    • nir-aham-stambhaḥ — freed from the pillar of false ego
      Compound: nir- (without) + aham (I) + stambha (pillar, post). Ahaṁkāra is pictured as a stiff pillar that wealth feeds; poverty saws through it. Gauḍīya frame: nirahaṁkāra is the soil in which prapatti finally takes root.
    • muktaḥ — liberated
      Past participle from √muc, 'to release.' Used here in a preliminary, ego-level sense — not mokṣa proper, but freedom from one specific bondage (false prestige). Gauḍīya distinction: this is the entry-level mukti from which bhakti-mukti begins.
    • yadṛcchayā — by chance, from providence
      Same word as in SB 10.10.5 — there for the descent of the sādhu, here for the supply of food. Gauḍīya frame: the same divine spontaneity that sends Nārada also sends the pauper's daily bowl. Providence is Kṛṣṇa's calligraphy.
    • tapaḥ — austerity
      From √tap, 'to heat, burn.' Austerity is a controlled burn of the lower nature. The verse equates forced privation with voluntary tapas only in effect, not in mood — a tapas one chooses for Kṛṣṇa retains its bhakti-flavor; one merely endured at least burns ahaṅkāra.
    A poverty-stricken man must automatically undergo austerities and penances because he does not have the wealth to possess anything. Thus his false prestige is vanquished. Always in need of food, shelter and clothing, he must be satisfied with what is obtained by the mercy of providence. Undergoing such compulsory austerities is good for him because this purifies him and completely frees him from false ego.
    Purport

    A saintly person voluntarily accepts a state of poverty just to become free from material false prestige. Many great kings left their princely standard of living and went to the forest to practice austerity according to Vedic culture, just to become purified. But if one who cannot voluntarily accept such austerity is put into a situation of poverty, he automatically must practice austerity. Austerity is good for everyone because it frees one from material conditions. Therefore, if one is very much proud of his material position, putting him into poverty is the best way to rectify his foolishness. Dāridrya-doṣo guṇa-rāśi-nāśi: when a person is poverty-stricken, naturally his false pride in aristocracy, wealth, education and beauty is smashed. Thus corrected, he is in the right position for liberation.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    A poverty-stricken man must automatically undergo austerities and penances because he does not have the wealth to possess anything. Thus his false prestige is vanquished. Always in need of food, shelter and clothing, he must be satisfied with what is obtained by the mercy of providence. Undergoing such compulsory austerities is good for him because this purifies him and completely frees him from false ego.
    Commentary

    When one is poor, automatically one practices detachment suitable for liberation. This is expressed in three verses. The poor person is free from lack of humility stemming from pride in wealth (nirahamstabha) and free from pride in family and education.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The poor man is devoid of arrogance arising from pride in wealth (nirahaṁ-stambhaḥ). He is freed from agitation of the heart arising from all things related to wealth (sarva-madaiḥ muktaḥ). He experiences suffering such as lack of food by the nature of poverty (yadṛcchayā). That suffering is the best austerity because it destroys his pride. Like the best type of austerity, poverty cannot be the cause of pride.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The poor man becomes humble (stambhaḥ), free of pride in wealth (niraham). Or the poor man becomes devoid of the causes (stambhaḥ) of pride (wealth and power). By this he becomes the opposite of the wealthy man who does not consider his aging body etc. By the nature of poverty, he experiences suffering like hunger. Poverty is the best remedy because it destroys pride.

    Personal Guidance
    Forced poverty does the work of voluntary tapas — it strips the false ego built on wealth, birth, and beauty, leaving you fit for surrender to Kṛṣṇa.
    Practical Applications
    • Identify one prop of false prestige today — title, salary, a possession — and refuse to mention or lean on it in a single conversation where you normally would.
    • Voluntarily accept one small inconvenience (a plainer meal, a longer walk, a cheaper option) and receive it as Kṛṣṇa's mercy rather than a hardship.
    • When something is taken from you today — money, comfort, recognition — name it aloud as tapas and thank Kṛṣṇa for the chance it gives you to drop ahaṅkāra.
    Analogy

    An ascetic vows to eat once a day, sleep on the ground, and own one cloth — tapas chosen for bhakti. A pauper is forced into the same regimen by circumstance. The bodies undergo the same austerities; whether ahaṅkāra is burned out or merely fermented depends on which mood the man brings to the privation.

    Stories
    Raghunātha dāsa Gosvāmī's renunciation

    Born to immense Bengali wealth and married to a beautiful wife, Raghunātha dāsa repeatedly fled his palace to join Mahāprabhu. After his final escape, in Vraja, he reduced his food to nearly nothing, slept under a tree, and spent his hours weeping and chanting.

    What the world saw as poverty was, in Caitanya-caritāmṛta, the highest tapas — voluntary stripping of every prop of false ego. SB 10.10.15 describes the forced version that does the same work without the choice; Raghunātha shows what the freely chosen version looks like in mādhurya-rasa.

    Important Words
    • kṣut — hunger
      Nominative of kṣudh. Treated here functionally — hunger as the senses' pacifier when there is nothing to feed them. Gauḍīya ascetic practice channels the same physiology by choice: light meals, simple food, prasāda only.
    • indriyāṇi — the senses
      Nominative plural of indriya, 'belonging to Indra' — the senses are Indra's domain, the gateway of enjoyment. Bhakti redirects indriyas to sevā; tapas (here forced) weakens them so they cannot lead the man astray.
    • anuśuṣyanti — become weaker
      Present plural from anu-√śuṣ, 'to dry up gradually.' The verb is metaphorically apt — senses 'dry' when not watered with viṣaya. Gauḍīya frame: the goal is not dried senses, but senses irrigated by Kṛṣṇa-sevā instead of viṣaya-rasa.
    • hiṁsā — envy, the tendency to harm
      From √hiṁs, 'to injure.' The verse traces a chain: weak body → quiet senses → reduced hiṁsā. Gauḍīya ahiṁsā ultimately rests not on physical weakness but on seeing every jīva as Kṛṣṇa's part — but this verse names the lower entry-point honestly.
    Always hungry, longing for sufficient food, a poverty-stricken man gradually becomes weaker and weaker. Having no extra potency, his senses are automatically pacified. A poverty-stricken man, therefore, is unable to perform harmful, envious activities. In other words, such a man automatically gains the results of the austerities and penances adopted voluntarily by saintly persons.
    Purport

    According to the opinion of experienced medical practitioners, diabetes is a result of voracious eating, and tuberculosis is a disease of undereating. We should desire neither to be diabetic nor to be tubercular. Yāvad artha-prayojanam. We should eat frugally and keep the body fit for advancing in Kṛṣṇa consciousness. As recommended elsewhere in Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (1.2.10) : kāmasya nendriya-prītir lābho jīveta yāvatā jīvasya tattva-jijñāsā nārtho yaś ceha karmabhiḥ The real business of human life is to keep oneself fit for advancement in spiritual realization. Human life is not meant for making the senses unnecessarily strong so that one suffers from disease and one increases in an envious, fighting spirit. In this Age of Kali, however, human civilization is so misled that people are unnecessarily increasing in economic development, and as a result they are opening more and more slaughterhouses, liquor shops and brothels. In this way, the whole civilization is being spoiled.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Always hungry, longing for sufficient food, a poverty-stricken man gradually becomes weaker and weaker. Having no extra potency, his senses are automatically pacified. A poverty-stricken man, therefore, is unable to perform harmful, envious activities. In other words, such a man automatically gains the results of the austerities and penances adopted voluntarily by saintly persons.
    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The result of his suffering is that he controls his senses. Desiring food, such persons completely dry up their senses. This means that they become disinterested in the taste of sense objects. Thus they give up violence to others for the purpose of enjoying the senses objects. By pride in wealth one loses control of the senses this leads to violence. When the opposite condition, poverty, occurs, violence disappears and one gains control of the senses.

    Personal Guidance
    Voluntary frugality (yāvad artha-prayojanam) does for the body what poverty forces — quiets the senses and frees energy for Kṛṣṇa consciousness.
    Practical Applications
    • Eat one meal today at the threshold of sufficiency, not satisfaction — notice how your senses settle when the body is not overfed.
    • Refuse the next purchase or indulgence whose only purpose is to strengthen sense-enjoyment, and redirect that time to japa or śravaṇam.
    • Before each meal, ask whether this food is fueling tattva-jijñāsā or merely feeding indriya-prīti, and adjust the portion accordingly.
    Analogy

    An overfed horse paws and bolts; the same horse, fed only what the work requires, walks calmly under the rider. The senses are the same horse; portions decide whether they carry you to Kṛṣṇa or run you off the road. Yāvad-artha eating is the bridle.

    Stories
    Sanātana Gosvāmī's mādhukarī

    Sanātana Gosvāmī, formerly prime minister of Bengal, lived in Vṛndāvana on alms collected like a bee — a little flour from one door, salt from another, never enough to fill the stomach. He survived on a single dry capātī cooked on a fragment of clay.

    When a wealthy disciple offered him richer food, he refused. The body was kept exactly at sufficiency, no more — and the result was the immense literary corpus of Hari-bhakti-vilāsa and Bṛhad-bhāgavatāmṛta. SB 10.10.16 names the principle; Sanātana writes the demonstration.

    Important Words
    • sādhavaḥ — saintly persons
      Nominative plural of sādhu. From √sādh, 'to accomplish.' The sādhu is one who has accomplished the goal of life — sambandha realized, abhidheya practiced, prayojana being lived. Their saṅga is itself the means.
    • sama-darśinaḥ — equal-visioned
      Compound: sama (equal) + darśin (one who sees). Sādhus see all jīvas as parts of Kṛṣṇa equally — but the pauper is the one positioned to receive that equal vision, because his pride is already broken. Gītā 5.18 uses the same compound.
    • tarṣam — the desire for material enjoyment
      Accusative of tarṣa, 'thirst.' Bhakti-rasāmṛta-sindhu uses tṛṣṇā as the same root metaphor. Sat-saṅga is the only liquid that quenches tarṣa — material indulgence merely brines it. The verse promises the thirst itself will reduce.
    • viśuddhyati — is cleansed
      Present middle from vi-√śudh, 'to purify thoroughly.' The intensifier vi- matters: not surface washing but core cleansing. The same verb Gauḍīya tradition uses for what saṅkīrtana does to the heart (ceto-darpaṇa-mārjanam).
    Saintly persons may freely associate with those who are poverty-stricken, but not with those who are rich. A poverty-stricken man, by association with saintly persons, very soon becomes uninterested in material desires, and the dirty things within the core of his heart are cleansed away.
    Purport

    It is said, mahad-vicalanaṁ nṝṇāṁ gṛhiṇāṁ dīna-cetasām ( Bhāg. 10.8.4 ). The only business of a saintly person or sannyāsī, a person in the renounced order, is to preach Kṛṣṇa consciousness. Sādhus, saintly persons, want to preach to both the poor and the rich, but the poor take more advantage of the sādhus’ preaching than the rich do. A poor man receives sādhus very quickly, offers them obeisances, and tries to take advantage of their presence, whereas a rich man keeps a big greyhound dog at his door so that no one can enter his house. He posts a sign saying “Beware of Dog” and avoids the association of saintly persons, whereas a poor man keeps his door open for them and thus benefits by their association more than a rich man does. Because Nārada Muni, in his previous life, was the poverty-stricken son of a maidservant, he got the association of saintly persons and later became the exalted Nārada Muni. This was his actual experience. Therefore, he is now comparing the position of a poor man with that of a rich man. satāṁ prasaṅgān mama vīrya-saṁvido bhavanti hṛt-karṇa-rasāyanāḥ kathāḥ taj-joṣaṇād āśv apavarga-vartmani śraddhā ratir bhaktir anukramiṣyati ( Bhāg. 3.25.25 ) If one gets the advantage of association with saintly persons, by their instructions one becomes more and more purified of material desires. kṛṣṇa-bahirmukha haiyā bhoga-vāñchā kare nikaṭa-stha māyā tāre jāpaṭiyā dhare ( Prema-vivarta ) Material life means that one forgets Kṛṣṇa and that one increases in one’s desires for sense gratification. But if one receives the advantage of instructions from saintly persons and forgets the importance of material desires, one is automatically purified. Ceto-darpaṇa-mārjanaṁ bhava-mahā-dāvāgni-nirvāpaṇam ( Śikṣāṣṭaka 1). Unless the core of a materialistic person’s heart is purified, he cannot get rid of the pangs of bhava-mahā-dāvāgni, the blazing fire of material existence.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Saintly persons may freely associate with those who are poverty-stricken, but not with those who are rich. A poverty-stricken man, by association with saintly persons, very soon becomes uninterested in material desires, and the dirty things within the core of his heart are cleansed away.
    Commentary

    One should not think that if the poor man has only one desire, that is enough to cause his downfall. He has some relief. The devotees are equal to the rich and poor, and therefore visit both out of mercy. In the presence of the devotee the poor man develops a relationship through the possibility of worship and discussion. This bears good results. This does not result from the devotees’ association with the man intoxicated with wealth. By the power of the devotee’s association (sadbhih), the desire in the poor man is weakened. By the mercy of the devotee what remains is the taste for the nectar of devotion. Verse 15 mentioned the poor man by fate (yadrcchaya) received suffering. But the devotee does not get that suffering and bhakti by karma , for the devotee has no karma.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    However he becomes successful by association with devotees. The devotees meet the poor person without making effort (yujyante) since both parties are prone to wander around in solitary places. The word eva indicates that they meet with the poor man only, not with the wealthy man. It is rare that the devotee goes to the wealth man since his house is crowded with people. The devotees do not make efforts to meet the wealthy man and avoid the poor man like other people do. They see wealth or lack of it equally (sama-darśinaḥ). By association with the devotees, the poor man quickly (ārāt) loses all thirst for other objects. Some versions have hi śuddhyati. Hi means certainly.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    However he becomes successful by association with devotees. The devotees think of the lord and the poor man as equals, but not the rich man, and associate with the poor man (yujyante) because they cannot die taking wealth with them. Or they associate with the poor to give them benefit, since they are compassionate to the suffering people. Or sama means the Lord who associates (sa) with Lakṣmī (mā). The devotees, fixed on seeing the Lord (sama-darśinaḥ), associate with the poor man because they are similar in not having wealth. Thus they are more merciful to the poor. By the devotees the person very quickly (ārāt) destroys his constant greed for food or attachment to enjoyment. That is certain (hi).

    Personal Guidance
    Wealth builds walls against sādhus; poverty keeps the door open — seek their saṅga so the heart's dirt is washed and material tarṣa quietly dies.
    Practical Applications
    • Notice today which 'greyhound at the door' — money, status, busyness — you use to keep the association of devotees at arm's length, and dismantle one of them.
    • Spend at least fifteen minutes in actual saṅga today — hear from a sādhu in person, on a recorded class, or through Prabhupāda's purports — and let the instruction touch one specific material desire.
    • Refuse to romanticize your comforts; identify one area where your relative 'richness' is dulling your hunger for Kṛṣṇa, and voluntarily simplify it this week.
    Analogy

    Sādhus pass through a city like wind through a screen — there is no door for them at the rich man's palace, but the pauper's torn curtain catches them and they sit down. Poverty is the screen's tear; through it the breeze of sat-saṅga reaches the heart's room.

    Stories
    Vidura at Maitreya's hermitage

    Vidura, having abandoned the Kuru court and his nephew Dhṛtarāṣṭra's palace, set out on pilgrimage as a poor wanderer. Stripped of position, he met the sage Maitreya by the Yamunā and received in those days the entire teaching that became SB Canto 3 — Sāṅkhya, Kapila-Devahūti, the cosmology of the universe.

    While he was a palace minister, no such instruction had reached him. Once he became daridra — the very condition Nārada commends in SB 10.10.17 — the sādhu's words filled the space where royal duty had been.

    Important Words
    • mukunda-caraṇa-eṣiṇām — whose only business is to serve Mukunda's feet
      Compound: Mukunda (giver of mukti, Kṛṣṇa) + caraṇa (feet) + eṣin (one who seeks). The whole identity of a sādhu in one compound. Gauḍīya frame: sādhu is not defined by renunciation or learning but by what his feet are seeking — Kṛṣṇa's feet, exclusively.
    • dhana-stambhaiḥ — with the rich and proud
      Compound: dhana (wealth) + stambha (pillar, stiffness). The same stambha that nirahaṁ-stambha (SB 10.10.15) undoes. Wealth makes a man stiff — incapable of bowing, therefore incapable of receiving sādhu-saṅga.
    • asadbhiḥ — with non-devotees
      Instrumental plural of asat — the same word from SB 10.10.12. The chapter weaves sat (sādhu) and asat (the rich-proud) through every verse: who you walk beside is who you become.
    • asat-āśrayaiḥ — taking shelter of non-devotees
      Compound: asat + āśraya (shelter). The opposite of śaraṇāgati. Bhakti's foundational choice is named by its negative: where you do not take shelter is half of where you do. Gauḍīya prayers explicitly renounce asat-āśraya.
    Saintly persons [sādhus] think of Kṛṣṇa twenty-four hours a day. They have no other interest. Why should people neglect the association of such exalted spiritual personalities and try to associate with materialists, taking shelter of nondevotees, most of whom are proud and rich?
    Purport

    A sādhu is one who is engaged in devotional service to the Lord without deviation ( bhajate mām ananya-bhāk ). titikṣavaḥ kāruṇikāḥ suhṛdaḥ sarva-dehinām ajāta-śatravaḥ śāntāḥ sādhavaḥ sādhu-bhūṣaṇāḥ “The symptoms of a sādhu are that he is tolerant, merciful and friendly to all living entities. He has no enemies, he is peaceful, he abides by the scriptures, and all his characteristics are sublime.” ( Bhāg. 3.25.21 ) A sādhu is suhṛdaḥ sarva-dehinām, the friend of everyone. Why then should the rich, instead of associating with sādhus, waste their valuable time in association with other rich men who are averse to spiritual life? Both the poor man and the rich man can take advantage of the Kṛṣṇa consciousness movement, and here it is advised that everyone do so. There is no profit in avoiding the association of the members of the Kṛṣṇa consciousness movement. Narottama dāsa Ṭhākura has said: sat-saṅga chāḍi’ kainu asate vilāsa te-kāraṇe lāgila ye karma-bandha-phāṅsa If we give up the association of sādhus, saintly persons engaged in Kṛṣṇa consciousness, and associate with persons seeking sense gratification and accumulating wealth for this purpose, our life is spoiled. The word asat refers to an avaiṣṇava, one who is not a devotee of Kṛṣṇa, and sat refers to a Vaiṣṇava, Kṛṣṇa’s devotee. One should always seek the association of Vaiṣṇavas and not spoil one’s life by mixing with avaiṣṇavas. In Bhagavad-gītā (7.15) , the distinction between Vaiṣṇava and avaiṣṇava is enunciated: na māṁ duṣkṛtino mūḍhāḥ prapadyante narādhamāḥ māyayāpahṛta-jñānā āsuraṁ bhāvam āśritāḥ Anyone who is not surrendered to Kṛṣṇa is a most sinful person ( duṣkṛtī ), a rascal ( mūḍha ), and the lowest of men ( narādhama ). Therefore one should not avoid the association of Vaiṣṇavas, which is now available all over the world in the form of the Kṛṣṇa consciousness movement.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Saintly persons [sādhus] think of Kṛṣṇa twenty-four hours a day. They have no other interest. Why should people neglect the association of such exalted spiritual personalities and try to associate with materialists, taking shelter of nondevotees, most of whom are proud and rich?
    Commentary

    With the wealthy man, identifying with his wealth, the devotee develops no relationship. Those non vaisnavas (asadbhih) afflicted by pride due to wealth (dhana stambhaih), who associate and serve non vaisnavas (asad asrayaih), are given up (upeskyaih) by the devotees. However, the devotees associate with those wealthy persons who are free of pride, and serve vaisnavas.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    “Let the devotees not associate with the wealthy for earning money, but let them associate to give mercy to them.” Devotees are fixed in proper conduct (sādhūnām). The materialists are fixed in improper conduct since it seen they indulge in women, gambling and liquor. The devotees see both the poor and the wealthy with the same vision. The materialists see with unequal vision because of their pride in wealth. The devotees take shelter of the Lord alone since they desire the feet of the Lord. The materialists take shelter of material objects since they desire enjoyment. Because the temperaments are opposite, the materialists have no attraction for the devotees (upekṣyaiḥ). What is the use of showing mercy to persons who are not qualified for mercy offered with great effort?

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    “Will the wealthy ever get association with the devotees by their wealth? Those who have good conduct, who have peaceful hearts or who know about ātmā (sama-cittānām), and who desire the feet of the Lord who gives bliss which derides liberation (mukunda), have nothing to do with the indifferent persons, persons who are proud of wealth, persons of bad conduct or who give shelter to persons of bad conduct. The order of the three types of devotees is increasingly excellent. Or all the phrases describe one type of person, the devotee of Mukunda, who has a peaceful heart and good conduct.

    Personal Guidance
    Sādhus live absorbed in Mukunda's feet — why squander our hours among the proud and rich (asat), when their company costs us our soul?
    Practical Applications
    • Audit today's calendar and cut one slot of asat-saṅga — the conversation that runs only on wealth, status, or sense-pleasure — and replace it with even fifteen minutes of devotee association, in person or by reading Prabhupāda.
    • Notice the moment you feel small around someone's money or position; remember a sādhu is suhṛdaḥ sarva-dehinām, and refuse to bow inside to dhana-stambha (pride of wealth).
    • Speak to one Vaiṣṇava today about Kṛṣṇa — call, message, or visit — and treat that exchange as more valuable than any networking with non-devotees.
    Analogy

    The bee leaves the honey-rich flower for the open field — why? Because the field has the next flower, the next, and Mukunda's lotus feet at the end. To leave the sādhu's wide field for the dhana-stambha rich man's closed orchard is to trade the journey for a single sterile bloom.

    Stories
    Caitanya Mahāprabhu and Sārvabhauma Bhaṭṭācārya

    When Mahāprabhu came to Jagannātha Purī, Sārvabhauma Bhaṭṭācārya — the most learned and well-positioned scholar in the city — attempted to instruct Him in impersonal Vedānta. Mahāprabhu listened in silence for seven days.

    Finally He gave His own explanation of the ātmārāma verse (SB 1.7.10), reaching the personalist conclusion. Sārvabhauma's dhana-stambha (pride of learning, equivalent to wealth) collapsed; he became a humble Vaiṣṇava and composed the Sārvabhauma-śatakam. SB 10.10.18 names dhana-stambha as the obstacle; Caitanya-līlā shows the obstacle being dissolved by sādhu-saṅga itself.

    straiṇayoḥ
    because they have become so attached to women
    ajita - ātmanoḥ
    being unable to control the senses .
    Important Words
    • mādhvyā — by sweet liquor (Mādhvī)
      Instrumental of mādhvī, a liquor distilled from honey. The very word madhu (sweet) is contaminated here — anything sweet to the senses without Kṛṣṇa becomes intoxicating in the wrong sense. Gauḍīya distinction: only Kṛṣṇa-līlā is mādhurya unmixed.
    • vāruṇyā — by liquor named Vāruṇī
      Instrumental of vāruṇī — the heavenly liquor reappears, named explicitly. Nārada lists the specific intoxicants because the cure must address each. Gauḍīya practice replaces vāruṇī with caraṇāmṛta — same act of drinking, opposite consequence.
    • tamaḥ-madam — false prestige due to the mode of ignorance
      Compound: tamas + mada. The deepest of the three madas the chapter names — beyond rajo-guṇa drunkenness (SB 10.10.8), there is tamo-guṇa pride that does not even know it is fallen. The curse aims precisely at this final layer.
    • hariṣyāmi — I shall take away
      Future first person from √hṛ, 'to take, remove.' The same root as hari (one who takes away sins). Nārada acts as Hari's hand: he removes the very thing his patient values most, because that is the disease.
    • ajita-ātmanoḥ — of those unable to control the senses
      Dual genitive of compound seen in SB 10.10.9. The diagnosis repeats — the disease is consistent. Gauḍīya frame: ajita-ātmā cannot become jita-ātmā by force of will alone; sādhu-saṅga and Vaiṣṇava chastisement together do the work.
    Therefore, since these two persons, drunk with the liquor named Vāruṇī, or Mādhvī, and unable to control their senses, have been blinded by the pride of celestial opulence and have become attached to women, I shall relieve them of their false prestige.
    Purport

    When a sādhu chastises or punishes someone, he does not do so for revenge. Mahārāja Parīkṣit had inquired why Nārada Muni was subject to such a spirit of revenge ( tamaḥ ). But this was not tamaḥ, for Nārada Muni, in full knowledge of what was for the good of the two brothers, wisely thought of how to cure them. Vaiṣṇavas are good physicians. They know how to protect a person from material disease. Thus they are never in tamo-guṇa. Sa guṇān samatītyaitān brahma-bhūyāya kalpate ( Bg. 14.26 ). Vaiṣṇavas are always situated on the transcendental platform, the Brahman platform. They cannot be subject to mistakes or the influence of the modes of material nature. Whatever they do, after full consideration, is meant just to lead everyone back home, back to Godhead.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Therefore, since these two persons, drunk with the liquor named Vāruṇī, or Mādhvī, and unable to control their senses, have been blinded by the pride of celestial opulence and have become attached to women, I shall relieve them of their false prestige.
    Commentary

    What then is the cure for their disease of pride? After considering, Narada decided on the cure. That is presented in four verses. Madhya means sweet. Tamo means ignorance. "I will remove the ignorance of these two intoxicated with sweet wine, blinded by pride in wealth, overly attached to women."

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    “Their intoxication will be over shortly.” Since they are permanently blinded by pride in their wealth, they will become repeatedly intoxicated with liquor. They are also addicted to women. “By enjoying these things their addiction will cease.” No, it will not, because they have uncontrolled minds.

    Personal Guidance
    A true Vaiṣṇava acts not from tamas but from compassion — Nārada's curse on the proud, intoxicated brothers is medicine to break their false prestige.
    Practical Applications
    • Notice today where wealth, position, or sensory indulgence is quietly making you 'drunk' — name one specific pride and refuse to feed it.
    • When a sādhu, scripture, or honest friend chastises you, receive it as a physician's prescription rather than as an attack on your ego.
    • Before correcting someone in your own life, pause and ask whether you are acting from revenge (tamas) or from real compassion for their soul — speak only if it is the latter.
    Analogy

    A father, seeing his sons drunk and exposing themselves before guests, does not coddle them — he locks them out of the wine cellar and stands them under cold water in the courtyard. Nārada's curse is exactly this cold-water treatment: humiliating on contact, sobering by morning.

    Stories
    Prahlāda before Hiraṇyakaśipu

    Prahlāda, a small boy, faced his father Hiraṇyakaśipu — the most opulent and intoxicated emperor in three worlds — and refused to renounce Viṣṇu. He spoke plainly, without spite, naming his father's śrī-mada and tamo-mada for what they were.

    The wrath that fell on him was severe (poison, weapons, elephants, fire), but Prahlāda's words were never tamasika — they were the same anugraha-arthāya speech Nārada uses in SB 10.10.19. A pure devotee's correction wounds the false self only to wake the true one.

    Important Words
    • tamaḥ-plutau — drowned in darkness
      Compound: tamas + plutau (the two flooded). From √plu, 'to swim, be flooded.' The image is hydraulic — they are not partially in tamas but submerged in it. The tree-body forces stillness on what was a flood.
    • sthāvaratām — immobility (state of a tree)
      From sthāvara (stationary). Śāstra divides life into sthāvara (immobile — plants, trees) and jaṅgama (mobile — animals, humans). The demotion is precise: those who used mobility for hiṁsā lose mobility itself.
    • smṛtiḥ — remembrance
      From √smṛ, 'to remember.' The mercy embedded in the curse. Without smṛti the punishment would be merely karmic; with smṛti it becomes the soil for bhakti. Gauḍīya: smaraṇa is the third anga of bhakti — Nārada plants it forcibly.
    • mat-prasādena — by my mercy
      Instrumental compound. Prasāda from a Vaiṣṇava is non-different from Kṛṣṇa's prasāda — Nārada speaks here as the channel. The curse and the mercy share a single instrumental, because in a pure devotee the two are one act.
    • vāsudevasya — of Vāsudeva (Kṛṣṇa)
      Genitive of Vāsudeva — Kṛṣṇa as son of Vasudeva, the personal Lord in full sweetness. Not Paramātmā in abstract; the verse names Him by His family relation. Nārada is already pointing forward to the dāmodara-līlā that will close the chapter.
    • labdha-bhaktī — having regained devotional service
      Compound: labdha (regained) + bhakti. Bhakti is treated as something that can be 'regained' — implying it is the jīva's svarūpa-dharma, only temporarily covered. Gauḍīya frame: jīva is by nature kṛṣṇera nitya-dāsa; bhakti is restored, not invented.
    These two young men, Nalakūvara and Maṇigrīva, are by fortune the sons of the great demigod Kuvera, but because of false prestige and madness after drinking liquor, they are so fallen that they are naked but cannot understand that they are. Therefore, because they are living like trees (for trees are naked but are not conscious), these two young men should receive the bodies of trees. This will be proper punishment. Nonetheless, after they become trees and until they are released, by my mercy they will have remembrance of their past sinful activities. Moreover, by my special favor, after the expiry of one hundred years by the measurement of the demigods, they will be able to see the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Vāsudeva, face to face, and thus revive their real position as devotees.
    Purport

    A tree has no consciousness: when cut, it feels no pain. But Nārada Muni wanted the consciousness of Nalakūvara and Maṇigrīva to continue, so that even after being released from the life of trees, they would not forget the circumstances under which they had been punished. Therefore, to bestow upon them special favor, Nārada Muni arranged things in such a way that after being released, they would be able to see Kṛṣṇa in Vṛndāvana and thus revive their dormant bhakti. Each day of the demigods in the upper planetary system equals six months of our measurement. Although the demigods in the upper planetary system are attached to material enjoyment, they are all devotees, and therefore they are called demigods. There are two kinds of persons, namely the devas and the asuras. Asuras forget their relationship with Kṛṣṇa ( āsuraṁ bhāvam āśritāḥ ), whereas the devas do not forget. dvau bhūta-sargau loke ’smin daiva āsura eva ca viṣṇu-bhaktaḥ smṛto daiva āsuras tad-viparyayaḥ ( Padma Purāṇa ) The distinction between a pure devotee and a karma-miśra devotee is this: a pure devotee does not desire anything for material enjoyment, whereas a mixed devotee becomes a devotee to become a first-class enjoyer of this material world. One who is in direct touch with the Supreme Personality of Godhead in devotional service remains pure, uncontaminated by material desires ( anyābhilāṣitā-śūnyaṁ jñāna-karmādy-anāvṛtam ). By karma-miśra-bhakti one is elevated to the celestial kingdom, by jñāna-miśra-bhakti one is able to merge in the Brahman effulgence, and by yoga-miśra-bhakti one is able to realize the omnipotency of the Supreme Personality of Godhead. But pure bhakti does not depend on karma, jñāna or yoga, for it simply consists of loving affairs. The liberation of the bhakta, therefore, which is called not just mukti but vimukti, surpasses the five other kinds of liberation — sāyujya, sārūpya, sālokya, sārṣṭi and sāmīpya. A pure devotee always engages in pure service ( ānukūlyena kṛṣṇānuśīlanaṁ bhaktir uttamā ). Taking birth in the upper planetary system as a demigod is a chance to become a further purified devotee and go back home, back to Godhead. Nārada Muni indirectly gave Maṇigrīva and Nalakūvara the greatest opportunity by his so-called curse.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    These two young men, Nalakūvara and Maṇigrīva, are by fortune the sons of the great demigod Kuvera, but because of false prestige and madness after drinking liquor, they are so fallen that they are naked but cannot understand that they are. Therefore, because they are living like trees (for trees are naked but are not conscious), these two young men should receive the bodies of trees. This will be proper punishment. Nonetheless, after they become trees and until they are released, by my mercy they will have remembrance of their past sinful activities. Moreover, by my special favor, after the expiry of one hundred years by the measurement of the demigods, they will be able to see the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Vāsudeva, face to face, and thus revive their real position as devotees.
    Commentary

    Stavaratam means that they deserve to be in bodies that cannot move, ie trees because they manifest those qualities: being naked, not performing proper action (not moving), and not speaking (properly). But even in this state they will be able to keep their memory by my mercy. After a hundred of the deva years (divya saraccate), they will meet Vasudeva and, developing prema bhakti, will attain their original bodies as devas.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Since the two were sons of Kuvera but became covered with ignorance, and, out of great pride, did not even recognize their nakedness before me, it is proper that they become trees so that they will not act in this manner again. However, by my mercy they will retain their memory and by Kṛṣṇa’s mercy to me, they will attain association with Kṛṣṇa after a hundred divine years, attain steady bhakti and return to their planet. The two, born as sons of a devatā, have been covered with ignorance. They are naked, not just because of ignorance but because of pride. They have ignored me and thus committed offense. “What is the offense in being naked in front of that brāhmaṇa?” This attitude arose because of greatly sinful pride. Because of faulty actions (ataḥ) they should become trees, since they were filled with ignorance. Having become most poor as trees, they will not act like this again. “There are many trees. They will not be given any teachings.” They will remember their previous lives. They will do service to the people of Vraja. Hari-vaṁśa says yau tāv arjuna-vṛkṣau tu vraje satyopayācanau: the two arjuna tress prayed for service in Vraja. Because Kṛṣṇa is merciful to me, they will attain association with him, after a hundred devatā years, since only after that would Kṛṣṇa appear. They will attain bhakti. He made this blessing because the devotees never give any blessing except bhakti. Attaining bhakti means that they would attain steady bhakti at that point.

    Personal Guidance
    Even Nārada's curse becomes mercy: Kṛṣṇa preserves memory through punishment so the fallen can revive bhakti when they finally see Him.
    Practical Applications
    • Notice today which 'curse' in your life — a setback, a humbling, a forced stillness — is actually Kṛṣṇa's arrangement to strip away false prestige and restore remembrance of Him.
    • Refuse to numb the consciousness of your past mistakes; sit with the memory deliberately, the way Nārada left Nalakūvara and Maṇigrīva their smṛti, so the lesson ripens into bhakti.
    • When you catch yourself drunk on position, talent, or status, stop and ask aloud: 'Am I standing naked like a tree without knowing it?' — then offer that pride at Kṛṣṇa's feet before the day ends.
    Analogy

    A goldsmith does not throw the gold ornament away when it is bent — he heats it, hammers it back, and polishes it. Nārada heats Nalakūvara and Maṇigrīva in the fire of arboreal stillness, hammers them with the memory of their fall, and finally polishes them with the promised darśana of Vāsudeva. Punishment is the goldsmith's intention all along.

    Stories
    Ajāmila

    Ajāmila, fallen brāhmaṇa, lived a life of crime and concubinage. At death the Yamadūtas came; in terror he called the name of his youngest son Nārāyaṇa. The Viṣṇudūtas appeared and drove the Yamadūtas off — the chance utterance had been registered.

    Spared, Ajāmila spent his remaining years in tapas at Hardvar and was liberated. SB 6.1–3 stages the same logic as the yamala-arjuna episode: a fallen jīva preserved in consciousness long enough to encounter Bhagavān or His name, then redeemed. Nārada's mat-prasādena... smṛtiḥ syāt is Ajāmila's whole story compressed into one phrase.

    Important Words
    • devarṣiḥ — the great saint Nārada
      Nominative of devarṣi — repeating the title from SB 10.10.5. The verse closes Nārada's appearance with the same address it opened with: he came as devarṣi, acted as devarṣi, departs as devarṣi. Consistency of svarūpa across action.
    • nārāyaṇa-āśramam — to his own āśrama, Nārāyaṇa-āśrama
      Compound: Nārāyaṇa + āśrama (hermitage). Nārada's residence is named after Nārāyaṇa Himself — his external life is non-different from his upāsya. Gauḍīya frame: the devotee's place of residence is Vaikuṇṭha-extension because his consciousness is Vaikuṇṭha-extension.
    • yamala-arjunau — twin arjuna trees
      Compound: yamala (twin) + arjuna (the tree, white-barked, terminalia arjuna). Their new identity is announced at the verse's close. Gauḍīya tradition reads even the species — arjuna, also Pārtha's name — as foreshadowing the personal encounter with Kṛṣṇa to come.
    Śukadeva Gosvāmī continued: Having thus spoken, the great saint Devarṣi Nārada returned to his āśrama, known as Nārāyaṇa-āśrama, and Nalakūvara and Maṇigrīva became twin arjuna trees.
    Purport

    Arjuna trees are still found in many forests, and their skin is used by cardiologists to prepare medicine for heart trouble. This means that even though they are trees, they are disturbed when skinned for medical science.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Śukadeva Gosvāmī continued: Having thus spoken, the great saint Devarṣi Nārada returned to his āśrama, known as Nārāyaṇa-āśrama, and Nalakūvara and Maṇigrīva became twin arjuna trees.
    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    This verse shows that he had come at his own will. They were born at the same time (yamala—couple) as arjuna trees. Since arjuna would also be the name of Kṛṣṇa’s cowherd friend in Vraja that they got the same name was his mercy. Thus making them arjuna trees as described in this verse was Nārada’s mercy.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Nārada went to Vaikuṇṭha (nārāyaṇāśramam). Thinking he made amgreat offense by cursing the servants of Śiva, he went there to get forgiveness, or to pray that his words would come true. Or he went to Badarikāśrama since he was ashamed to meet the Lord directly, feeling a direct request was inappropriate. He went there to request his guru, who had descended there. Or he went to see the Lord there out of devotion. He would inform his guru of what he had done by chance on the way. They were born at the same time (yamala—couple) as arjuna trees. Since arjuna would also be the name of Kṛṣṇa’s cowherd friend in Vraja, that they got the same name was his mercy. Thus making them arjuna trees as described in this verse was Nārada’s mercy.

    Personal Guidance
    Even cursed in tree-form, Nalakūvara and Maṇigrīva await Kṛṣṇa's touch — no condition is so fallen that the Lord's mercy cannot reach and reclaim it.
    Practical Applications
    • Notice one area today where you feel 'stuck like a tree' — rooted in habit — and offer that exact stuckness to Kṛṣṇa rather than waiting to first improve it.
    • When you encounter another being's suffering — even a plant being skinned for medicine — let it remind you that consciousness pervades all bodies and respond with ahiṁsā in some small choice.
    • Refuse to despair over a long-standing fault; instead, do one concrete sādhana act today (chant, hear, serve) trusting that the same Lord who liberated the yamala-arjunas reaches you too.
    Analogy

    An archer, having loosed his arrow with perfect aim, simply lowers the bow and walks home — he does not need to follow the shaft to its target. Nārada lets fly the curse, sees that it has lodged correctly, and returns to Nārāyaṇa-āśrama. The shaft will do its work without him.

    Important Words
    • bhāgavata-mukhyasya — of the topmost of devotees
      Compound: bhāgavata (devotee of Bhagavān) + mukhya (foremost). The verse names Nārada with his Vaiṣṇava qualification, not his demigod station. Bhāgavata-mukhya is the chapter's structural counterpoint to dhana-stambha — what truly entitles a being to Kṛṣṇa's action.
    • satyam — truthful
      From √as, 'to be.' Satya is what is, what endures. Kṛṣṇa makes the devotee's word satya — the Lord lends His own being to confirm what His pure devotee has spoken. The hierarchy of truth: Kṛṣṇa supports the devotee's word; the devotee supports the disciple's word.
    • hariḥ — Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Personality of Godhead
      Nominative of Hari — 'one who removes.' He removes sins, illusions, and bondage. The naming is deliberate: it is Hari who walks to the trees, because the action is removal — of the curse-as-tree, of the long-standing material covering.
    • śanakaiḥ — very slowly
      Instrumental plural used adverbially. The toddler's pace. Gauḍīya commentators (Sanātana, Viśvanātha) dwell on this word: omnipotence walking slowly, because slowness is what the līlā requires for Yaśodā to chase, for the rope to lengthen, for the trees to be reached at the right moment.
    The Supreme Personality of Godhead, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, to fulfill the truthfulness of the words of the greatest devotee, Nārada, slowly went to that spot where the twin arjuna trees were standing.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    The Supreme Personality of Godhead, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, to fulfill the truthfulness of the words of the greatest devotee, Nārada, slowly went to that spot where the twin arjuna trees were standing.
    Commentary

    The preparations for fulfilling the curse are related in this verse.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Having described the history, Śukadeva now shows what Kṛṣṇa did when he remembered that the two sons of Kuvera were trees, which was described previously. (SB 10.9.23) It was proper that Nārada’s words should come true. Kṛṣṇa began to make this happen. Another version has bhāgavatas tasya instead of bhāgavata-mukhyasya. Nārada is called thus because he is most worthy of worship for having the highest type of knowledge, bhakti. Hariḥ (to take away) indicates that the Lord wanted to deliver the two from the curse. He went slowly because he feared the sound that he produced would bring his mother and others. Or he did this slowly because he was a small child. Also the mortar would not come loose if it was pulled gently. He crawled so that he could pull the mortar strongly. This is mentioned in the Second Canto: yad riṅgatāntara-gatena divi-spṛśor vā unmūlanam: simply by his crawling between the two arjuna trees which touched the heavens, he uprooted them. (SB 2.7.27)

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Kṛṣṇa wanted to fulfil the words of his great devotee. He would deliver the two from the curse (hariḥ). He moved quickly because he feared that the sound of dragging the mortar would bring Yaśodā and others. Or he did not want to show his quick movements in pulling the huge mortar, since he was still a small child. He was also crawling while pulling the mortar with strength yad riṅgatāntara-gatena divi-spṛśor vā unmūlanaṁ tv itarathārjunayor na bhāvyam || Simply by his crawling between the two Arjuna trees which touched the heavens, he uprooted them. (SB 2.7.27)

    Personal Guidance
    Kṛṣṇa Himself walks slowly to the yamala-arjuna trees to honor His devotee Nārada's words — He moves to make a bhakta's vāṇī true.
    Practical Applications
    • Today, keep one small word you have given — to a parent, child, or friend — and recognize Kṛṣṇa's pleasure in honoring a devotee's speech.
    • Notice where you treat your own promises as negotiable, and refuse to let convenience break what your tongue has committed.
    • When you read or hear a sādhu's instruction, act on it that same day — trust that Kṛṣṇa Himself moves to fulfill the words of His devotees.
    Analogy

    A young king, knowing the gardener has promised to receive him at noon, slows his walk so the gardener's word will be made true at the appointed hour. Kṛṣṇa, omnipotent, walks śanakaiḥ — slowly — across Yaśodā's courtyard so Nārada's curse can ripen exactly into its prophesied moment. The Lord is His devotee's footman.

    Stories
    Kṛṣṇa and Vidura's khichaḍī

    On His diplomatic mission to Hastināpura, Kṛṣṇa was offered lavish feasts by Duryodhana and refused them all. He went instead to Vidura's modest hut and ate simple meal — and according to one tradition, in His absorption He ate even the banana skins Vidura's wife handed Him by mistake.

    The Supreme Personality of Godhead arranged His own movements to honor His devotee's hospitality. SB 10.10.24 shows the same protocol on a larger scale: Kṛṣṇa walks slowly so Nārada's word will be fulfilled. The Lord's omnipotence has a single rule it submits to — bhakta-vānī.

    Important Words
    • priya-tamaḥ — most beloved devotee
      Compound: priya (dear) + superlative -tama. The hierarchy of Kṛṣṇa's affection is named in one word — among many priyas, Nārada is priya-tama. Gauḍīya: every devotee is dear, but bhāgavata-mukhya level is Kṛṣṇa's intimate preference.
    • dhanada-ātmajau — the two sons of Kuvera
      Compound: dhanada (wealth-giver, Kuvera) + ātmaja (son). Kṛṣṇa names them by their material lineage and immediately sets it aside as no qualification. Birth and wealth do not summon Kṛṣṇa; the devotee's wish does.
    • sādhayiṣyāmi — I shall accomplish
      Future first person from √sādh — the same root as sādhu. Kṛṣṇa 'accomplishes' the devotee's words; the same root names the sādhu who has 'accomplished' the goal. Word and Lord share grammar.
    • mahātmanā — by the great soul (Nārada)
      Instrumental of mahātman, 'great-souled.' Gītā 9.13 reserves mahātmā for the unalloyed devotee. Kṛṣṇa here uses the title for Nārada in the same sense — the title is bhakti's, not philosophy's.
    “Although these two young men are the sons of the very rich Kuvera and I have nothing to do with them, Devarṣi Nārada is My very dear and affectionate devotee, and therefore because he wanted Me to come face to face with them, I must do so for their deliverance.”
    Purport

    Nalakūvara and Maṇigrīva actually had nothing to do with devotional service or seeing the Supreme Personality of Godhead face to face, for this is not an ordinary opportunity. It is not that because one is very rich or learned or was born in an aristocratic family one will be able to see the Supreme Personality of Godhead face to face. This is impossible. But in this case, because Nārada Muni desired that Nalakūvara and Maṇigrīva see Vāsudeva face to face, the Supreme Personality of Godhead wanted to fulfill the words of His very dear devotee Nārada Muni. If one seeks the favor of a devotee instead of directly asking favors from the Supreme Personality of Godhead, one is very easily successful. Śrīla Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura has therefore recommended: vaiṣṇava ṭhākura tomāra kukkura bhuliyā jānaha more, kṛṣṇa se tomāra kṛṣṇa dite pāra. One should desire to become like a dog in strictly following a devotee. Kṛṣṇa is in the hand of a devotee. Adurlabham ātma-bhaktau . Thus without the favor of a devotee, one cannot directly approach Kṛṣṇa, what to speak of engaging in His service. Narottama dāsa Ṭhākura therefore sings, chāḍiyā vaiṣṇava-sevā nistāra pāyeche kebā: unless one becomes a servant of a pure devotee, one cannot be delivered from the material condition of life. In our Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava society, following in the footsteps of Rūpa Gosvāmī, our first business is to seek shelter of a bona fide spiritual master ( ādau gurv-āśrayaḥ ).

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    "Although these two young men are the sons of the very rich Kuvera and I have nothing to do with them, Devarṣi Nārada is My very dear and affectionate devotee, and therefore because he wanted Me to come face to face with them, I must do so for their deliverance."
    Commentary

    Because (yat) Narada is my dear devotee, I will give fulfill to these two whatever (yad) was said by that (tad) great soul (mahatmana).

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Because Nārada is my great devotee I will do just as he sung -deliver them from tree bodies, have them go to Svarga, and endow them with the highest bhakti.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    I will do just as was described by my great devotee (mahātmanā), dedicated to spreading my bhakti by his nature. This was the cause of his being dear to the Lord (priyatamaḥ). I will free them from bodies of trees and give them the highest bhakti (sādhayiṣyāmi). They will be devotees.

    Personal Guidance
    Kṛṣṇa reveals Himself not by wealth, birth, or learning, but through the mercy of His pure devotee — seek the devotee, and Kṛṣṇa is already in your hand.
    Practical Applications
    • Identify one bona fide Vaiṣṇava in your life and serve him today in some small, concrete way — fetch, clean, listen, write — without waiting to be asked.
    • Refuse the subtle pride of approaching Kṛṣṇa on the strength of your own qualifications; instead, pray through a devotee, asking him to remember you.
    • Notice when you bypass guru and Vaiṣṇavas to manufacture a private relationship with Kṛṣṇa, and re-route that impulse into ādau gurv-āśrayaḥ — taking shelter first.
    Analogy

    A king grants audience not because the petitioner is rich, but because his trusted minister has put in a good word. Kṛṣṇa explicitly says: I have nothing to do with these two — but Nārada is My priya-tama, and his word brings them to My presence. The minister's reference is the only credential that matters.

    Stories
    Nārada and Dhruva

    When the five-year-old Dhruva, stung by his stepmother's insult, set out for the forest to seek the Lord, it was Nārada who met him on the road, tested his resolve, and gave him the mantra oṁ namo bhagavate vāsudevāya — the one mantra that would bring Viṣṇu to him.

    Six months of tapas later, Viṣṇu appeared. Dhruva himself had no qualification; Nārada's mantra was the bridge. SB 10.10.25 names the same principle Kṛṣṇa Himself will state again in Caitanya-caritāmṛta — guru-kṛṣṇa-prasāde pāya bhakti-latā-bīja.

    Important Words
    • antareṇa — between
      Indeclinable, 'in the middle of.' The exact placement matters: Kṛṣṇa positions Himself precisely between the trees. Gauḍīya commentators note that He is always antara-yāmin (the inner controller) — externally He enacts antara as a spatial position.
    • yamayoḥ — of the twins
      Genitive dual of yama — twin. The trees are addressed by the same root that names Yamarāja, lord of death. The trees are a death-state (sthāvaratā); Kṛṣṇa enters between the twin deaths to reveal their hidden life.
    • ātma-nirveśa-mātreṇa — as soon as He entered
      Compound: ātman + nirveśa (entry) + mātra (the mere measure of). 'By the mere fact of entering.' Kṛṣṇa exerts no effort; His presence alone is the lever. Gauḍīya: His līlā always carries this lightness — no strain, only sweetness.
    • tiryak — crossways
      Indeclinable. The single word that performs the entire līlā — the mortar turns sideways and lodges. Sanskrit's economy: one syllable carries the mechanical pivot of the whole episode.
    Having thus spoken, Kṛṣṇa soon entered between the two arjuna trees, and thus the big mortar to which He was bound turned crosswise and stuck between them.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Having thus spoken, Kṛṣṇa soon entered between the two arjuna trees, and thus the big mortar to which He was bound turned crosswise and stuck between them.
    Commentary

    Thinking in this way he went between the pair of trees (yamau). Just as he entered between the trees, the mortar became crooked.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    He thought “For this purpose the two offenders have become trees, for participating in my childhood pastimes.” Then he crawled towards the trees. The mortar was pulled at right angles by his will. Tiryak means crooked or obliquely. One version has bhṛtam. This suggests the mortar was conscious by being related to the Lord. Or all articles in the Lord’s pastimes are eternity, knowledge and bliss. That applies to the rope also. Otherwise they could not possibly be related to the Lord who is eternity, knowledge and bliss. Hari-vaṁśa says tad dāma tasya prabhav ād abhavat drḍham: by his power the rope became strong. PadmaPurāṇa says namas te tu dāmne sphurad dīpti- dhāmne: I offer respects to the shining rope.

    Personal Guidance
    Kṛṣṇa wedges Himself between the twin arjuna trees — His apparent bondage is the very setup for liberating those who have been bound for ages.
    Practical Applications
    • Notice today where what feels like a constraint on you is actually Kṛṣṇa positioning Himself to break a long-standing bondage in your life.
    • Refuse to read setbacks as evidence of His absence — bring one such situation before Him this evening and ask what He is dragging into the open.
    • Speak to Kṛṣṇa directly about a 'stuck' relationship or pattern you have endured for years, and trust His timing to turn it crosswise and crack it open.
    Analogy

    A child working a wedge between two stuck logs — push it crossways and the logs split apart. Kṛṣṇa, dragging the wooden mortar behind Him, slips between the twin trees and turns the mortar crosswise; the bondage of a hundred celestial years splits open in an instant. The wedge is small; the cleaving is total.

    Important Words
    • bālena — by the boy Kṛṣṇa
      Instrumental of bāla — a small child. The verse names the agent as a toddler precisely to highlight the disjunction. Gauḍīya rasa: it is in vātsalya-līlā that aiśvarya is most piquantly veiled.
    • dāma-udareṇa — by the one with a rope on His belly
      Compound: dāma (rope) + udara (belly). The name Dāmodara is born here — eternal in Vraja, but the chapter is its etymological source. Gauḍīya: Dāmodara is Kṛṣṇa as supremely controllable by His devotee's love.
    • parama-vikramita — by supreme power
      Compound: parama (supreme) + vikrama (heroic stride). The same vikrama by which Vāmana strode the universe; here exerted by an infant against two trees. The scale changes; the agent does not.
    • utkalita — uprooted
      Past participle from ut-√kal, 'to dig up.' Not snapped, not pushed over — uprooted. The metaphor reaches forward to the uprooting of long-standing material attachments that Vaiṣṇavas pray Dāmodara to perform inside their hearts.
    By dragging behind Him with great force the wooden mortar tied to His belly, the boy Kṛṣṇa uprooted the two trees. By the great strength of the Supreme Person, the two trees, with their trunks, leaves and branches, trembled severely and fell to the ground with a great crash.
    Purport

    This is the pastime of Kṛṣṇa known as dāmodara-līlā. Therefore another of Kṛṣṇa’s names is Dāmodara. As stated in the Hari-vaṁśa: sa ca tenaiva nāmnā tu kṛṣṇo vai dāma-bandhanāt goṣṭhe dāmodara iti gopībhiḥ parigīyate

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    By dragging behind Him with great force the wooden mortar tied to His belly, the boy Kṛṣṇa uprooted the two trees. By the great strength of the Supreme Person, the two trees, with their trunks, leaves and branches, trembled severely and fell to the ground with a great crash.
    Commentary

    The two trees were pulled out by the roots by Damodara who was pulling the mortar which followed him with great force. With trunk, branches and leaves shaking (ativepa) because of the great force of pulling (parama vikramita), the two trees fell over. According to the Hari Vamsa he is called Damodara because of being bound up: sa ca tenaiva namna tu krsno vai damobandhanat gosthe damodara iti gopibhih parigiyate.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The two trees, uprooted by Dāmodara, who pulled constantly (niṣ) the mortar which was turned sideways, fell down completely (niṣ), with force. The branches (viṭapau), leaves and trunks trembled violently. Or the phrase may be divided differently: Param avikramitātivepa-skandha-pravāla-vitapau: the branches, leaves and trunks did not tremble too much. His name Dāmodara indicates his sweetness. Uprooting the trees indicates his power. As previously, his sweetness hides his powers. Hari-vaṁśa explains his name. sa ca tenaiva nāmnā tu kṛṣṇo vai dāmbandhanāt goṣthe dāmodara iti gopībhiḥ parigīyate Because he was bound by rope Kṛṣṇa is called Dāmodara by the gopīs in Vraja.

    Personal Guidance
    Even bound by a mother's rope, Kṛṣṇa uproots what binds us — surrender to His sweetness, and He breaks the trees of our long-standing attachments.
    Practical Applications
    • Name one 'tree' rooted in your life — a long-standing attachment or pride — and offer it explicitly to Dāmodara in your morning prayer today.
    • When you feel small, bound, or dragged through your duties, remember the dāmodara-līlā: it is precisely in being 'tied' that Kṛṣṇa reveals His mercy — do your bound duty with that bhāva.
    • Refuse to measure spiritual progress by your own strength; let one task today be done with the conscious admission, 'only His parama-vikrama uproots what I cannot.'
    Analogy

    A child seems to drag a rope tied to His belly; in fact a kingdom of bondage is being uprooted with each step. The same boy who lets Himself be tied is the one whose parama-vikrama splits century-old trunks. Sweetness and supremacy are not in tension in Kṛṣṇa's līlā — they are the same step seen from two sides.

    Stories
    Hanumān uprooting the mountain

    When Lakṣmaṇa lay unconscious from Indrajit's astra, Hanumān flew to Gandhamādana for the sañjīvanī herb. Unable to identify it, he uprooted the entire mountain and brought it to Laṅkā.

    SB 10.10.27 stages the same parama-vikrama in toddler form: Kṛṣṇa uproots two mountain-old trees while tied to a mortar. The same Supreme Person who, as Rāma's servant, lifted Gandhamādana, here in His own svayaṁ-rūpa lifts entire trees as if they were grass. The Gauḍīya reading is exact: Hanumān serves the Lord, the Lord enacts the Hanumān-level strength inside His own līlā.

    Important Words
    • siddhau — two perfect persons
      Nominative dual of siddha. From √sidh, 'to be accomplished.' The same root as sādhu. Their identity is announced — they are no longer guhyaka-yakṣas, they are siddhas. The fall has become the ascent.
    • jāta-vedāḥ — fire personified
      Compound: jāta (born) + vedas (knowledge) — an epithet of Agni, who is 'born with knowledge.' Their effulgence is Vedic — they emerge with vidyā restored, no longer the avidyā-blind sons of Kuvera.
    • akhila-loka-nātham — controller of all worlds
      Compound: akhila (entire) + loka (worlds) + nātha (master). The toddler is recognized as Lord of all worlds. Gauḍīya: aiśvarya-jñāna can erupt in vātsalya-līlā when the recipient is a newly-liberated soul — Yaśodā does not see this, the siddhas do.
    • baddha-añjalī — with folded hands
      Compound: baddha (bound) + añjali (the hollowed-hand gesture). The first physical act of bhakti — añjali is the body's grammar of surrender. Gauḍīya: ātma-nikṣepa, one of the six aṅgas of śaraṇāgati, is embodied in añjali.
    • virajasau — fully cleansed of the mode of ignorance
      Compound: vi- (without) + rajas (passion/dust). 'Dustless.' One word reverses the entire opening of the chapter, where they were drunk, naked, and rolling-eyed. Same beings, no rajas left.
    Thereafter, in that very place where the two arjuna trees had fallen, two great, perfect personalities, who appeared like fire personified, came out of the two trees. The effulgence of their beauty illuminating all directions, with bowed heads they offered obeisances to Kṛṣṇa, and with hands folded they spoke the following words.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Thereafter, in that very place where the two arjuna trees had fallen, two great, perfect personalities, who appeared like fire personified, came out of the two trees. The effulgence of their beauty illuminating all directions, with bowed heads they offered obeisances to Kṛṣṇa, and with hands folded they spoke the following words.
    Commentary

    The two persons emerging from the trees (kujayoh) lit up the four directions (kakubho) with their bodily light which mixed together like one fire (jatatvedah).

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Two devatās were situated (siddhau) in the two trees (tatra). They shone in all directions (kakubhaḥ) with beauty. Or they made the directions splendid with beauty. Or, coming from a distance close to Kṛṣṇa, they glowed because of his effulgence. They bowed down, touching their heads to the ground (pra-namya) quickly, so that their faces were not visible. Kṛṣṇa was still pulling the mortar. “Why did they offer respects to Kṛṣṇa who has playing as a small child, Dāmodara?” They realized he was the lord of the whole universe. By the mercy of Nārada, they gained that realization. Or the question may be asked “Why did the two, given memory by the mercy of Nārada, though they were great offenders, give up shame and come to the side of the Lord?” They came because he was the shelter of all beings. They were now devoid of offense (virajasau). Sma indicates astonishment. Though they were great offenders, suddenly they attained such a status.

    Personal Guidance
    Once Kṛṣṇa's mercy frees you from your inherited entanglements, the only fitting response is bowed-head, folded-hand surrender to Him as Lord of all.
    Practical Applications
    • Recall one entanglement Kṛṣṇa has already quietly removed from your life, and offer praṇāma in gratitude before you begin the day's work.
    • When a long-standing material attachment finally falls away, refuse to credit your willpower — fold your hands inwardly and acknowledge Kṛṣṇa as akhila-loka-nātha.
    • Before speaking your next request to Kṛṣṇa, first bow the head and offer praise — let surrender precede petition, as Nalakūvara and Maṇigrīva did.
    Analogy

    Two flames hidden inside dark logs leap free when the wood splits — bright, headed-bowed, hands folded, recognizing the splitter as their deliverer. So Nalakūvara and Maṇigrīva emerge as jāta-vedāḥ from their tree-prison and bow at the toddler's feet. The first act of any freed soul is praṇāma.

    Stories
    Gajendra's surrender

    Gajendra, the elephant king, was seized by the crocodile in the lake. After a thousand celestial years of struggle, he finally raised a single lotus in his trunk and offered prayers to the unseen Lord. Viṣṇu Himself appeared and freed him.

    The Bhāgavatam records (SB 8.3) Gajendra's first act on emerging: he composed and offered prayers to Hari. SB 10.10.28 stages the same pattern — liberation is not an end-state but a beginning of stuti. The siddhāḥ emerge with bowed heads and folded hands, because liberation expresses itself as obeisance.

    Important Words
    • kṛṣṇa kṛṣṇa — O Kṛṣṇa, O Kṛṣṇa
      Vocative repeated. The name is the prayer; doubling intensifies the cry. Gauḍīya: this verse is one of the scriptural seeds of nāma-saṅkīrtana — the freed soul's first utterance is Kṛṣṇa's name, twice.
    • mahā-yogin — O master of mysticism
      Compound: mahā (great) + yogin (one possessed of yoga). Kṛṣṇa is yogeśvara — the Lord of all yogic potency. The infant is addressed by His highest title; the freed siddhas see no contradiction.
    • ādyaḥ — the original
      From √ad — 'the first.' Gauḍīya: kṛṣṇas tu bhagavān svayam (SB 1.3.28) — Kṛṣṇa is svayaṁ-bhagavān, the original Person from whom all avatāras descend. The siddhas' address confirms the chapter's siddhānta.
    • puruṣaḥ — the Supreme Person
      Nominative of puruṣa. Gauḍīya distinguishes puruṣa-avatāras (Mahā-Viṣṇu, Garbhodakaśāyī, Kṣīrodakaśāyī) from Kṛṣṇa-svayam. Here puruṣa is qualified by ādya — the original Person, Kṛṣṇa Himself.
    • vyakta-avyaktam — manifest and unmanifest
      Compound: vyakta (manifest) + avyakta (unmanifest). The whole material cosmos in both phases is His rūpa. Gauḍīya frame: acintya-bhedābheda — the world is His energy, simultaneously one with and different from Him.
    O Lord Kṛṣṇa, Lord Kṛṣṇa, Your opulent mysticism is inconceivable. You are the supreme, original person, the cause of all causes, immediate and remote, and You are beyond this material creation. Learned brāhmaṇas know [on the basis of the Vedic statement sarvaṁ khalv idaṁ brahma] that You are everything and that this cosmic manifestation, in its gross and subtle aspects, is Your form.
    Purport

    The two demigods Nalakūvara and Maṇigrīva, because of their continuing memory, could understand the supremacy of Kṛṣṇa by the grace of Nārada. Now they admitted, “That we should be delivered by the blessings of Nārada Muni was all Your plan. Therefore You are the supreme mystic. Everything — past, present and future — is known to You. Your plan was made so nicely that although we stayed here as twin arjuna trees, You have appeared as a small boy to deliver us. This was all Your inconceivable arrangement. Because You are the Supreme Person, You can do everything.”

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    O Lord Kṛṣṇa, Lord Kṛṣṇa, Your opulent mysticism is inconceivable. You are the supreme, original person, the cause of all causes, immediate and remote, and You are beyond this material creation. Learned brāhmaṇas know [on the basis of the Vedic statement sarvaṁ khalv idaṁ brahma] that You are everything and that this cosmic manifestation, in its gross and subtle aspects, is Your form.
    Commentary

    Krsna could ask, "Why are you two who are devatas paying respects to me, a cowherd boy tied to a mortar?" They answer with this verse. The word Krsna is repeated twice to indicate that they spoke together. "You are the supreme person (parah purusah), bhagavan. But you, the cowherd boy, are the original, svayam bhagavan (adyah). Oh one who possess inconceivable power (mahayogin), whose bondage is not subject to logic, as you can liberate us, how is it possible for you , the form of the universe, to be bound up? With this intention they speak this verse.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    “Though we were great offenders, we have received your great mercy. What you have done is proper.” In this way they begin to speak. O parabrahman with human form (kṛsṇa)! They say his name twice out of great bliss or because of bewilderment of prema. However, it is the nature of the tongue to be attracted to Kṛṣṇa’s name. Or they repeated his name in order to have him face them, when they had attained a sober condition, since Kṛṣṇa was overwhelmed by his childhood pastime of pulling the mortar. O lord endowed with inconceivable and unlimited powers (mahā-yogin)! You are superior to Mahā-viṣṇu (puruṣaḥ paraḥ), the puruṣa who glances at prakṛti. You are his source. Though you are the source, you appear in many forms like Mahā-nārāyaṇa. Still you are Svayam Bhagavān (ādyaḥ). This is shown in the first verse of Brahma-saṁhitā: īśvaraḥ paramaḥ kṛṣṇaḥ. Because you are complete in qualities, this mercy you show us is suitable. Though you are Bhagavān, they know you as Brahman, the great form which is the basis of everything, or the effect—the universe. (brahmaṇaḥ rūpam). Another version has brāhmaṇāḥ (the brāhmaṇas know this). Your mercy is possible because we regard ourselves as your servants.

    Personal Guidance
    Kṛṣṇa is the ādya-puruṣa, the cause of all causes — the entire viśva, gross and subtle, is His form, and His arrangements are inconceivable.
    Practical Applications
    • When an unexpected reversal or rescue arrives today, name it aloud as Kṛṣṇa's inconceivable arrangement rather than chance or your own cleverness.
    • Open your day by addressing Him by name — 'Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa' — acknowledging Him as the supreme original person, not an impersonal force.
    • Look at one ordinary object — a tree, a meal, a stranger — and consciously see it as part of His vyakta-rūpa, His manifest form.
    Analogy

    A river-traveler, looking at the surface, sees only ripples and currents — but the boatman knows the bed beneath, the spring at the source, and the sea at the mouth. Kṛṣṇa is the river's source, riverbed, current, and sea. To see only the toddler-form (the surface) and miss the ādya-puruṣa (the source) is the human predicament; Nalakūvara and Maṇigrīva, freshly cleansed, see the whole length at once.
